Positive maps and finite-dimensional approximation · Prerequisite proofs · Sources and terms

Finite traces with arbitrary centers

Retained complete programme arguments PC0–7 and FCT0–7. Original programme exposition: CC0-1.0 to the extent of rights held; the same terms remain in force.

The projection comparison proof supplies the cancellation, central corners and arbitrary sums used to construct the trace. The construction proves existence, faithfulness and normal uniqueness for every finite von Neumann algebra, including nonseparable algebras and non-countably-decomposable centers. No scalar faithful trace or direct-integral decomposition is a starting assumption.

These complete proof sections come from the programme's projection comparison and center-valued trace lessons. The links to their earlier proofs below use the retained CF/SF/CP/ST foundations. The remaining sections of those larger lessons are outside this selected prerequisite route.

Projection comparison and the countably decomposable type III case

Independent exposition and original figure/source: CC0-1.0 to the extent of rights held.

Let M=M′′⊆B(H)M=M''\subseteq B(H)M=M′′⊆B(H), where HHH is any complex Hilbert space and the identity is 1H1_H1H​. Zero spaces are permitted. A projection is an element p=p∗=p2p=p^*=p^2p=p∗=p2. Write p∼qp\sim qp∼q if some v∈Mv\in Mv∈M has v∗v=p, vv∗=qv^*v=p,\ vv^*=qv∗v=p, vv∗=q, and p≾qp\precsim qp≾q if the final projection may instead be any subprojection of qqq. A projection ppp is finite if p∼q≤pp\sim q\leq pp∼q≤p forces q=pq=pq=p. Proper infiniteness means that p≠0p\neq0p=0 and every nonzero central compression of the unit of pMppMppMp is infinite. Type III means absence of nonzero finite projections. A projection is countably decomposable if every orthogonal family of its nonzero subprojections is countable.

The actual earlier mathematical inputs are CF Sections 1, 6–8 and 10, with Sections 2–5 as the continuous-calculus predecessors (choice/maximality, norm series, bounded C* calculus, Hilbert projection/adjoints/completion), SF-0 and SB-0 (the commutant-unitary test and elementary Hilbert facts), and CP-01–06 (concrete predual and vector-series topology). The polar construction below is the bounded specialization of the reviewed HA-R4 range-isometry argument, written completely here; its unbounded form theorem is not an additional input. No bounded or unbounded spectral representation theorem, weight theorem, trace existence, spectral classification or cardinal-dimension theorem is an input.

Free source comparison: Jesse Peterson's author notes, 2020, Sections 5.1–5.2, printed 83–90, and Brent Nelson's author notes, Lemma 5.2.9 and Proposition 5.2.13, printed 49–51. Every statement used in this proof is proved below or bound to the specified earlier programme proof. In particular the countability condition will concern only the projection to be embedded.

Actual earlier proof ranges: OA-FLOW.CF.1, OA-FLOW.CF.2, OA-FLOW.CF.3, OA-FLOW.CF.4, OA-FLOW.CF.5, OA-FLOW.CF.6, OA-FLOW.CF.7, OA-FLOW.CF.8, OA-FLOW.CF.10, OA-FLOW.SF.SF0, OA-FLOW.SF.SB0, OA-FLOW.CP.1, OA-FLOW.CP.2, OA-FLOW.CP.3, OA-FLOW.CP.4, OA-FLOW.CP.5, OA-FLOW.CP.6. Well-order III, and identify its cardinal with an infinite initial ordinal κ\kappaκ. The normalized trace with its full center retained

Let M⊆B(H)M\subseteq B(H)M⊆B(H) be a finite von Neumann algebra on an arbitrary complex Hilbert space, and put Z=Z(M)Z=Z(M)Z=Z(M). Finiteness means that an isometry in every projection corner has full final projection. Equivalently, the identity is a finite projection, since finiteness passes to subprojections by PC5. No countability, factor, separability or scalar-trace assumption is made.

We construct a unique normal positive linear map T:M→ZT:M\to ZT:M→Z such that

T(1)=1,T(zx)=zT(x),T(xy)=T(yx)(z∈Z, x,y∈M).(FCT1) T(1)=1,\qquad T(zx)=zT(x),\qquad T(xy)=T(yx) \quad(z\in Z,\ x,y\in M). \tag{FCT1}T(1)=1,T(zx)=zT(x),T(xy)=T(yx)(z∈Z, x,y∈M).(FCT1)

It is faithful, has norm one when M≠0M\ne0M=0, and preserves all bounded increasing positive suprema. Normal here means continuous on the entire concrete ultraweak space, not just on bounded sets. For the zero algebra the map is zero; its norm is zero and its normalization is T(0)=0T(0)=0T(0)=0.

The construction is quantitative: maps with trace distortion tending to one converge in operator norm. We prove that stability first, under an explicit tiling condition. We then supply the tilings, normal center-valued states and two local balancing arguments needed to produce those maps.

The earlier complete proofs used are CF1/3–8, SF0 and SB1–6, CP1–6, ST1–2, and PC1–7. Only the last automorphism corollary additionally uses the order-normal positive-map criterion NF6. Each use is located below. Scalar trace existence, type-I classification, direct integrals and a fixed-point theorem are not premises.

FCT7. Faithfulness, uniqueness and projection comparison

For every central tile in (FCT6), traciality and normalization give

T(p)=z/k.(FCT31) T(p)=z/k. \tag{FCT31}T(p)=z/k.(FCT31)

A nonzero projection qqq contains a nonzero tile ppp, so T(q)≥T(p)>0T(q)\ge T(p)>0T(q)≥T(p)>0. If x≥0x\ge0x≥0 is nonzero, some positive spectral cutoff q=1[δ,∞)(x)q=1_{[\delta,\infty)}(x)q=1[δ,∞)​(x) is nonzero; the squared-integral spectral identity would otherwise make x=0x=0x=0. Then T(x)≥δT(q)>0T(x)\ge\delta T(q)>0T(x)≥δT(q)>0. Thus TTT is faithful on the entire positive cone, and T(x∗x)=0T(x^*x)=0T(x∗x)=0 implies x=0x=0x=0.

Any other normal normalized center-valued trace has the same value (FCT31) on every central tile. FCT3 decomposes each projection into tiles, and normality identifies its value with their arbitrary positive sum. Therefore the two traces agree on all projections. Uniform spectral step approximation and boundedness then give equality on all self-adjoint elements and hence all of MMM. This is uniqueness among normal traces; it does not assume or assert normality of an arbitrary algebraic trace.

For projections, the full order criterion is

p≾q ⟺ T(p)≤T(q),p∼q ⟺ T(p)=T(q).(FCT32) p\precsim q\ \Longleftrightarrow\ T(p)\le T(q), \qquad p\sim q\ \Longleftrightarrow\ T(p)=T(q). \tag{FCT32}p≾q ⟺ T(p)≤T(q),p∼q ⟺ T(p)=T(q).(FCT32)

The forward implication uses the implementing partial isometry and positivity. Conversely PC2 splits centrally into zp≾zqzp\precsim zqzp≾zq and (1−z)q≾(1−z)p(1-z)q\precsim(1-z)p(1−z)q≾(1−z)p. On the second piece, place a copy of (1−z)q(1-z)q(1−z)q under (1−z)p(1-z)p(1−z)p. The positive residual has nonnegative trace, whereas T(p)≤T(q)T(p)\le T(q)T(p)≤T(q) makes its trace nonpositive. Faithfulness makes that residual zero, so the reverse subequivalence there is an equivalence. Add the two central implementations to get p≾qp\precsim qp≾q. Equality of traces gives both subequivalences; PC3 gives equivalence. This proof includes zero projections.

The support identity is sZ(T(p))=c(p)s_Z(T(p))=c(p)sZ​(T(p))=c(p): T(p)T(p)T(p) is supported on c(p)c(p)c(p); a central zzz annihilating T(p)T(p)T(p) gives T(zp)=0T(zp)=0T(zp)=0, hence zp=0zp=0zp=0 by faithfulness.

The converse existence assertion is also precise. If an arbitrary von Neumann algebra has a normal normalized center-valued trace, it is finite. Otherwise PC5 supplies a nonzero properly infinite central unit zzz, split as z=r+sz=r+sz=r+s with r∼s∼zr\sim s\sim zr∼s∼z. The trace law gives T(r)=T(s)=T(z)=zT(r)=T(s)=T(z)=zT(r)=T(s)=T(z)=z, while additivity gives T(z)=2zT(z)=2zT(z)=2z, a contradiction. After finiteness is established, the preceding construction and normal uniqueness prove that any such trace is faithful. No scalar-trace existence theorem was used to prove this implication.

Free method comparison

Jesse Peterson's author-hosted Notes on operator algebras, 27April2020, Section6.4, printed/PDF102–106, develops the approximate center-valued states and their norm-limit trace. FCT retains and credits that mathematical route. Its characterwise bound proves the norm of a positive central map for complex inputs; its explicit central tiles, cyclic compressions and summable preduals supply the type and arbitrary-assembly steps that the source method requires. Both occurrences of the balancing constant are retained.

The human source remains freely readable on its author's university page. Its text and PDF are not reproduced here or assigned the programme's licence. The complete programme comparison, bounded spectral calculus, predual and normal-range arguments are the actual earlier proof inputs.
